articles.title: About
articles.description: A bit more about me and my academic work.
articles.contents:
Background
I am a political science student with a strong interest in quantitative methods and data analysis. I enjoy using R and data visualization tools to explore political and social phenomena.
Through my coursework in GV300, I have developed skills in:
Data wrangling and cleaning with dplyr and tidyr
Statistical analysis and hypothesis testing
Data visualization with ggplot2
Reproducible research with R Markdown
This Website
This site was built using Distill for R Markdown and Postcards. It is hosted on GitHub Pages and serves as a portfolio for my academic work.
The landing page uses the Postcards package with the Trestles template.
The site is powered by Distill, a publication-quality format for scientific writing.
The GV300 showcase page demonstrates code and visualizations from my coursework.

articles.title: GV300 Showcase: Analysing the 2024 UK General Election
articles.description:
A showcase of my best code and visualisation from GV300, exploring
constituency sizes, voter turnout, and representation in the 2024 UK
General Election.
articles.contents:
Contents
Introduction
Data Preparation
Smallest and Largest Constituencies
Visualisation: Cross-Country Comparison
Summary Statistics by Country
Who Isn’t Voting?
Turnout by Category and Country
High vs Low Turnout Constituencies
Conclusion

Introduction
The 2024 UK General Election provides a rich dataset for examining how constituency sizes vary across the four nations, and how voter turnout differs between regions. In this showcase I present my best data-wrangling and visualisation code from GV300 Homework 2, where I analysed official candidate-level results published by the UK Parliament.
The analysis addresses three questions:
How much do constituency sizes vary, and what does that mean for equal representation?
Which visualisation best reveals cross-country differences?
Who isn’t voting, and where is turnout lowest?
Data Preparation
The code below loads the official 2024 candidacy-level CSV, cleans variable names, aggregates to constituency level, and computes a turnout measure.


Show code

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(stringr)

uk_csv <- "https://electionresults.parliament.uk/general-elections/6/candidacies.csv"
uk_raw <- read.csv(uk_csv, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# Standardise column names to lower_snake_case
names(uk_raw) <- names(uk_raw) %>%
  tolower() %>%
  str_replace_all("\\.", "_")

# Remove by-elections and keep key variables
uk1 <- uk_raw %>%
  filter(election_is_by_election == "false")

uk2 <- uk1 %>%
  select(
    constituency = constituency_name,
    country      = country_name,
    valid_votes  = candidate_vote_count,
    electorate   = electorate
  )

# Aggregate from candidate-level to constituency-level
uk3 <- uk2 %>%
  group_by(country, constituency) %>%
  summarise(
    valid_votes = sum(valid_votes, na.rm = TRUE),
    electorate  = max(electorate, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups     = "drop"
  )

# Compute turnout and drop invalid rows
uk <- uk3 %>%
  mutate(turnout_registered = 100 * valid_votes / electorate) %>%
  filter(is.finite(turnout_registered), electorate > 0)

knitr::kable(
  head(uk, 10),
  caption = "First 10 constituencies after cleaning",
  digits = 1
)

Show code

ratio <- max(uk$valid_votes) / min(uk$valid_votes)


The largest constituency has roughly 4.3 times as many valid votes as the smallest. Because each MP carries one vote in Parliament regardless of constituency size, voters in smaller constituencies effectively have more representation per person — raising questions about equal representation.
Visualisation: Cross-Country Comparison
A faceted histogram is a natural first attempt, but it is hard to compare across panels with different y-scales. A boxplot makes cross-country differences immediately visible on a single axis.


Show code

p_box <- ggplot(uk, aes(x = country, y = valid_votes / 1000, fill = country)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(
    title    = "Constituency Sizes by Country (2024 UK General Election)",
    subtitle = "Boxplots allow direct comparison of medians, spread, and outliers",
    x        = "Country",
    y        = "Valid Votes (thousands)",
    fill     = "Country"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.title      = element_text(face = "bold", size = 15),
    plot.subtitle   = element_text(color = "grey40"),
    legend.position = "none"
  )

print(p_box)



Summary Statistics by Country


Show code

size_summary <- uk %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  summarise(
    n_constituencies = n(),
    mean_votes       = mean(valid_votes),
    median_votes     = median(valid_votes),
    sd_votes         = sd(valid_votes),
    min_votes        = min(valid_votes),
    max_votes        = max(valid_votes),
    .groups          = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(mean_votes))

knitr::kable(
  size_summary,
  col.names = c("Country", "N", "Mean", "Median", "SD", "Min", "Max"),
  caption   = "Constituency sizes (valid votes) by country",
  digits    = 0,
  format.args = list(big.mark = ",")
)

Who Isn’t Voting?


Show code

non_voter_analysis <- uk %>%
  mutate(non_voters = electorate - valid_votes)

total_non_voters     <- sum(non_voter_analysis$non_voters)
total_electorate     <- sum(non_voter_analysis$electorate)
non_voter_percentage <- 100 * total_non_voters / total_electorate

top_non_voters <- non_voter_analysis %>%
  arrange(desc(non_voters)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10) %>%
  select(constituency, country, electorate, valid_votes, non_voters, turnout_registered)

Across all constituencies, approximately 19,414,872 registered voters did not vote — about 40.3% of the electorate. If non-voters are systematically different from voters (younger, poorer, more disengaged), then election outcomes may not reflect the preferences of the broader population.
Turnout by Category and Country


Show code

turnout_categories <- uk %>%
  mutate(
    turnout_category = case_when(
      turnout_registered < 55 ~ "Low",
      turnout_registered < 65 ~ "Medium",
      turnout_registered < 75 ~ "High",
      TRUE                    ~ "Very High"
    ),
    turnout_category = factor(
      turnout_category,
      levels = c("Low", "Medium", "High", "Very High")
    )
  )

category_counts <- turnout_categories %>%
  group_by(turnout_category, country) %>%
  summarise(n_constituencies = n(), .groups = "drop")

p_cats <- ggplot(category_counts,
                 aes(x = turnout_category, y = n_constituencies, fill = country)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Constituencies by Turnout Category",
    x     = "Turnout Category",
    y     = "Number of Constituencies",
    fill  = "Country"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.title      = element_text(face = "bold", size = 15),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )

print(p_cats)



High vs Low Turnout Constituencies


Show code

high_turnout <- uk %>% filter(turnout_registered > 70)
low_turnout  <- uk %>% filter(turnout_registered < 60)

high_summary <- high_turnout %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_electorate = mean(electorate),
    mean_turnout    = mean(turnout_registered),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(group = "High (>70%)")

low_summary <- low_turnout %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_electorate = mean(electorate),
    mean_turnout    = mean(turnout_registered),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(group = "Low (<60%)")

comparison <- bind_rows(high_summary, low_summary) %>%
  select(group, country, n, mean_electorate, mean_turnout)

knitr::kable(
  comparison,
  col.names = c("Group", "Country", "N", "Mean Electorate", "Mean Turnout (%)"),
  caption   = "Comparison of high- and low-turnout constituencies",
  digits    = 1,
  format.args = list(big.mark = ",")
)

Differences in turnout likely reflect socio-economic factors (deprivation, education), demographics (age structure), and political factors such as competitiveness and campaign intensity. Areas with greater political disengagement tend to exhibit lower turnout than places where voters are more engaged and parties campaign harder.
Conclusion
This analysis demonstrates the use of dplyr for data wrangling and ggplot2 for multi-dimensional visualisation. The boxplot and grouped bar chart effectively communicate cross-country differences in constituency size and voter turnout across the 2024 UK General Election.
Source code for this site is available at github.com/stasi1950/.github.io.

articles.title: GV300: Measurement, Reliability & Scale Construction
articles.description: An analysis of survey measurement quality, exploring institutional trust batteries, Cronbach's alpha reliability, scale construction, and cross-group comparisons using UK banking survey data.
articles.contents:
Introduction
This page showcases work from GV300 Homework 5, focusing on measurement, reliability, and validity in survey research. Using a UK banking/financial survey dataset, the analysis explores how well a battery of trust items hangs together, how to construct composite scales, and what patterns emerge across demographic groups.
Data and the Q37 Trust Battery
The Q37 battery asks respondents to rate their trust in 12 different institutions on a 0-10 scale. Most respondents cluster in the low-to-middle range. About 596 NAs per item appear to come from survey dropouts.
Missing Data
Only 46% of cases are complete across all 12 Q37 items. The NAs seem to come mainly from survey dropouts rather than selective non-response.
Reliability Cronbachs Alpha
Cronbach's alpha is approximately 0.92, well above the standard 0.7 threshold. The items are internally consistent.
Building Scales Sum vs Mean
The mean score stays on the original 0-10 scale, making it more interpretable and robust to partial missingness.
Cross-Group Comparison Trust by Education Level
Boxplots show institutional trust patterns across education levels from Below GCSE to Doctorate.
Research Design What Drives Trust in the Bank of England
A proposed research design using OLS regression to test whether central bank trust is shaped by personal financial circumstances, political opinions, or both.
